text: Antimatter vanishes the moment it touches anything. Yet in October twenty twenty-six, physicists reported holding one anti-electron, a positron, for months. <#0.5#> So they built a container with no walls. Magnetic and electric fields hold it in the middle, touching nothing. <#0.5#> One ancestor was a vacuum gauge. In nineteen thirty-six, Frans Penning used a magnet to measure almost-empty air. <#0.5#> Decades later, Dehmelt wrote that he wondered how to hold one electron still, then built a trap from Penning's gauge, and named it after him. <#0.6#> But holding one for months is not a first. Dehmelt's lab announced a positron named Priscilla, held in their trap for three months. <#0.9#> So what is new? Gabrielse's team cooled theirs almost to absolute zero, and can nudge it up one tiny energy step at a time. <#0.5#> The paper is published. The big test, matching it against an electron, is not done. <#0.6#> One particle, caged for months. Priscilla had a name. What would you call this one? <#1.0#>
